clue.text: Pool faucet repositioned in the wrong location

indicators.note: Letters that have been repositioned have been moved into new spots, so the fodder is rearranged.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A plumber has moved the tap by the swimming pool, and now it sits somewhere silly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's own complaint, a tap put in the wrong spot, is the definition, so the clue nearly describes its own answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain idiom: anything not where it belongs is said to be out of place.

clue.text: Unorthodox way a squash ball may be hit

definitions.meaning: eccentric, bizarre: an informal adjective for it

definitions.text: way a squash ball may be hit
definitions.meaning: in squash, players strike the ball so it rebounds from the court's front or side surfaces

explanation.surface: An odd shot on the squash court.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is literal: squash is played by bouncing the ball off the walls, and that phrase is also slang for weird.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal idiom for eccentric, plus the literal description of a squash rebound: both senses share one phrase.

clue.text: Couple ultimately don't show love

indicators.note: Ultimately means in the end, so each of the next words gives only its end letter.

parts.note: the last letters of DON'T and SHOW
love = O, a zero score in tennis

explanation.surface: A pair who, in the end, keep their affection hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: "Don't show love" reads as one phrase about a reserved pair; it splits into two words to be clipped and a zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a couple is a pair, a set of that number.

clue.text: Following a smart diet

parts.note: f. = following, as in page references (pp. 10 f.)
used as it stands
to smart = to hurt sharply, as a wound does

explanation.surface: Someone is on a clever new eating plan.
explanation.walkthrough: "Smart" looks like an adjective praising the diet; it is the verb, to hurt sharply.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: going without food is the most extreme eating regime.

clue.text: Start a filling daytime meal

indicators.note: A filling sits inside what it fills, so A goes into the meal.

parts.note: the midday meal, opened after its first letter
used as it stands, placed second

explanation.surface: Tuck into a hearty midday meal to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: "Filling" pretends to describe a substantial lunch; it is the instruction to put A inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to set a project or a ship going is to start it.

clue.text: Character appearing in Mission: Impossible?

parts.note: the surface wants a role in the spy film; the setter means a typed symbol
look at the printed title itself: one punctuation mark sits between its two words

explanation.surface: Which role turns up in the spy film Mission: Impossible?
explanation.walkthrough: "Character" suggests a person in the film; it is a typed character, the colon printed in its title.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword sense: a character is any typed symbol, and the two-dot mark sits in the title between Mission and Impossible.

clue.text: Acknowledge the audience and prepare for violin performance?

definitions.meaning: bend forward from the waist to thank the applause
a violinist picks up the stick strung with horsehair before playing

explanation.surface: A violinist bows to the crowd and then gets ready to play.
explanation.walkthrough: The same three words work twice: the bend at the end of a show, and the stick a violinist picks up.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for thanking an audience, and a literal reading where the bow is the violinist's stick.

clue.text: Failures in force leading to cuts

parts.note: F = force, the physics symbol
to lop = to cut off, as with branches

explanation.surface: A police force's failings are blamed on budget cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: "Leading to" is placing, not cause and effect: F leads, standing in front of the word for cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: shows or products that fail badly are called this.

clue.text: Transfer of data dumps Leonard periodically picked out

indicators.note: Periodically means at regular intervals, so letters are picked out at a steady rhythm.

parts.note: the 2nd and 4th letters: dUmPs
the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters, keeping the same rhythm across the gap

explanation.surface: Leonard picks items out of rubbish dumps now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words run together as one string, and every second letter from the second onward spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Computing term: sending files from a device up to a server is this kind of transfer.

clue.text: Very poor boys on trek getting lost

indicators.note: Hikers getting lost wander off their set route, so the letters leave their order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Some penniless lads lose their way on a long hike.
explanation.walkthrough: Stony-broke is British slang for having no money at all.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang synonym for penniless.

clue.text: Cover that's trimmed at both ends

indicators.note: Trimming cuts away the edges, and both ends means the first and last letters go.

parts.note: the word itself, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A cover with its edges cut back.
explanation.walkthrough: "That's" looks like grammar gluing the clue together; it is the word being trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by function: headgear covers the head.

clue.text: Individuals centrally involved in the actual act of stealing

indicators.note: Centrally means at the centre, so only the middle letter of the word is used.
To be involved in something is to be inside it, so that letter goes within the next word.

parts.note: used as it stands, opened up after its second letter
the middle (6th of 11) letter of INDIVIDUALS, placed after TH
very = actual, as in 'the very man'

explanation.surface: Some people are caught up in the middle of a real robbery.
explanation.walkthrough: "The actual act" reads as one phrase; split it after "the", which holds the I, and "actual" becomes VERY.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the noun for stealing, as larceny or theft.

clue.text: Working together live on stage?

definitions.meaning: a band recorded performing before an audience; the question mark flags the literal reading

explanation.surface: A band performing together in front of an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second sense is a playful literal reading of the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for acting jointly, and the literal sense of performing at a gig.

clue.text: Complaint with joint

parts.note: w = with, a standard abbreviation
the pivoting joint on a door or lid

explanation.surface: A grumble about an aching joint.
explanation.walkthrough: "Joint" suggests a sore knee; it is the door fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: British and Australian colloquial synonym for a moaning, peevish complaint.

clue.text: City living initially is good in Paris

indicators.note: Initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is taken.
What is said in Paris is said in French, so the word is translated.

parts.note: the first letter of LIVING
used as it stands
the French word for good

explanation.surface: Life in the city is good, says a Parisian.
explanation.walkthrough: The Paris in the surface is a decoy city; it only asks for French, and the answer is a different capital, Portugal's.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the capital of Portugal.

clue.text: Thorough department in one new hospital

indicators.note: One thing in another sits inside it, so the department's letters go within the rest.

parts.note: one = I, the Roman numeral
n = new, a standard abbreviation
H = hospital, as on road signs; DEPT sits between N and H
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: A thorough section of a newly built hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads a hospital department; each word there shrinks to an abbreviation instead: I N (DEPT) H.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a study that goes deep into its subject is thorough.

clue.text: Tipped to the side, like some significant buildings

definitions.meaning: what a ship does when it leans over in the water
in Britain, historic buildings are entered on an official register that protects them

explanation.surface: Grand old buildings are leaning over.
explanation.walkthrough: A listed building in Britain is one on the official register of historic buildings, so it cannot be altered freely.
explanation.definitionFit: Nautical verb for leaning, plus the British heritage term for a protected building.

clue.text: Issue arising from non-union activity?

parts.note: the surface wants a dispute; it means offspring
the surface wants work done without a trade union; the union is a marriage

explanation.surface: A dispute sparked by work done without the trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: The industrial-relations picture is false: "issue" means offspring, and a "union" here is a marriage, not a trade union.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphemism: a child born to unmarried parents, the issue of a non-marital union.

clue.text: What indicates slight pause in dialogue from sitcom, maybe?

definitions.text: What indicates slight pause in dialogue

indicators.note: Taken from means lifted straight out of the words that follow, letters unchanged.

parts.note: the last three letters of the first word and first two of the second

explanation.surface: What marks a short beat in a comedy script?
explanation.walkthrough: The printed comma in "sitcom, maybe" sits right where the hidden answer spans the break, a neat touch.
explanation.definitionFit: Punctuation by function: this mark tells a reader to take a brief breath.

clue.text: You and I primarily browse huge source of information online

parts.note: the pronoun for you and I together

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so only the first letter of the word is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of BROWSE

explanation.surface: Mostly we just surf the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: "Browse" and the definition both belong to the internet, so the surface keeps the wordplay and the answer in one scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Short name for the World Wide Web, the internet's vast store of pages.

clue.text: Input to AI tool executed without delay

definitions.meaning: the text a user types into a chatbot

explanation.surface: An instruction fed to a chatbot, carried out immediately.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sentence about a chatbot obeying; it splits into a noun and an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Modern computing noun for the instruction given to an AI, plus the adjective for punctual.

clue.text: Alcoholic drink in cup is cold

indicators.note: What is in a phrase sits inside it, so the answer is a run of letters within the words that follow.

parts.note: the letters run on unbroken across the words

explanation.surface: A drink served in a cup is chilled.
explanation.walkthrough: Pisco is a grape brandy from Peru and Chile. The answer runs from the last letter of 'cup' to the first two of 'cold'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a South American grape brandy.

clue.text: Understand where a bishop may have responsibilities

definitions.text: where a bishop may have responsibilities
definitions.meaning: a bishop's diocese, from the Latin for seat

explanation.surface: Grasping what a bishop's job covers.
explanation.walkthrough: A see is the district a bishop governs, named for the bishop's seat.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyday verb for grasping a point, plus the church term for a bishop's district.

clue.text: Tough cheddar?

definitions.meaning: the retort 'Tough!', meaning bad luck, in its British form
cheddar is a firm, pressed dairy product; the question mark flags an example

explanation.surface: A chewy lump of cheddar.
explanation.walkthrough: "Tough" reads as describing the cheese; it is the retort "Tough!", which the British also say as "Hard cheese!".
explanation.definitionFit: British idiom for tough luck, plus a literal description of cheddar by type.
